summary: For ages 5–7: the Arctic (North) and Antarctic (South) are two very different frozen places, not one 'cold everywhere'. The Arctic is a frozen OCEAN ringed by land (such as Canada, Alaska, Russia and Greenland); polar bears live there, and people (such as the Inuit) live on the surrounding lands. The Antarctic is a giant ICE-COVERED CONTINENT surrounded by ocean where penguins live and no people live permanently (only visiting scientists). The headline contrast to build is: polar bears live only in the far North, and wild penguins live only in the southern half of the world (many in and around Antarctica) — polar bears and penguins live at opposite ends of the Earth and never meet in the wild. Directly confront the common picture-book error of bears and penguins together. Core activities use a which-pole sorting action with corrective feedback; supporting activities add naming/where-they-live reveals, a globe for spatial 'top vs bottom', and a clean assessment check.
misconceptions: Polar bears and penguins live together (and polar bears eat penguins) — they live at opposite poles and never meet in the wild
The North and South Poles are basically the same place — one is ocean, the other is land
Penguins live at the North Pole / with Santa
The Arctic is a country or solid land like Antarctica — it is mostly a frozen ocean
People live at the South Pole all the time — only visiting scientists stay there temporarily

activities.title: Sort each animal and feature to its pole
steps: Look at two frozen scenes: a cracked, floating sea-ice ocean at the top of the world (Arctic) and a solid white ice-continent at the bottom (Antarctic).

Place picture cards onto the pole where each belongs: polar bear, penguin, walrus, a family in warm parkas, and the frozen sea at the North Pole. Then place a research hut card: scientists visit both poles, so it can go at either one — but in Antarctica it is the only kind of home people have.

Say WHY each card belongs there as you place it — for example, 'the bear lives on the frozen sea in the North', or 'families live in the Arctic all year round, but in Antarctica the only people are scientists who visit for a while and then go home'.

After sorting, look at the two scenes side by side and notice that every polar bear card is North and every penguin card is South — they never share a home — and that one pole floats on ocean while the other rests on land.
activities.insight: Which-pole-and-why is a sorting contrast: polar bears and their neighbours belong to the Arctic (frozen ocean, people live there), penguins to the Antarctic (ice continent, only temporary scientists), and the two never meet because they live at opposite ends of the Earth.

activities.title: Floating ice versus solid ground: ocean or land?
steps: Stand a toy polar bear on a piece of 'sea ice' floating on water in a bowl (the Arctic — a frozen ocean).
Stand a toy on a solid block of ice resting on a table (the Antarctic — an ice-covered land continent).
Describe the difference: at the North Pole the ice floats on the sea; in the Antarctic most of the ice sits on real land.
Match each pole to a simple cross-section picture: Arctic = frozen sea with land around it; Antarctic = land under ice with sea around it.
activities.insight: The two poles are not the same kind of place: the Arctic is mostly a frozen ocean, while the Antarctic is a land continent covered in ice.

activities.title: Top and bottom of the globe: tap to reveal who lives where
steps: Find the North Pole at the top of a globe or ball and the South Pole at the bottom.
On a split-screen North/South scene, tap each pole to reveal a fact: North shows polar bears, walruses and people in parkas; South shows penguins and a visiting scientist's hut.
Trace with a finger how far apart the two poles are — 'opposite ends of the Earth'.
activities.insight: North and South are opposite ends of the Earth; naming who lives at each pole reinforces that bears belong North and penguins belong South.

activities.title: Talk with a bear or penguin who has never met the other
steps: Chat with a friendly polar bear from the North (or a penguin from the South) who explains where it lives and who its neighbours are.
Ask the character whether it has ever met a penguin (or a polar bear), and hear why not — they live at opposite ends of the Earth.
Retell in your own words where the character lives and why the two animals never meet.
activities.insight: Polar bears and penguins live at opposite poles and never meet in the wild; one pole is a frozen ocean with people living on the lands around it, the other an ice continent where no people live permanently, only visiting scientists.

activities.title: Which pole? A check on the contrast
steps: Answer which-pole questions: 'Where do penguins live — North or South?', 'Which pole is a frozen ocean?'
Place a short set of animals and features into two columns, one for the Arctic and one for the Antarctic.
Answer: could a wild polar bear ever meet a wild penguin, and why or why not?
activities.insight: The learner can independently state the ocean-vs-continent difference and conclude that bears and penguins never meet.

checkQuestion: A friend says 'the Arctic and the Antarctic are basically the same — both freezing, both the same kind of place, and a polar bear could bump into a penguin at either one'. Is your friend right that they're the same? Tell me one big way the two places are DIFFERENT, and whether a wild polar bear and a wild penguin could ever meet.
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong. The Arctic (North) is a frozen OCEAN with land around it — polar bears, Arctic foxes and people like the Inuit live there. The Antarctic (South) is a huge LAND continent covered in ice, surrounded by ocean — penguins live there and no people live permanently. Because polar bears live only in the far North and penguins live only in the far South, a wild polar bear and a wild penguin could NEVER meet.
